hints: Look closely at the carbon on the far right of each ring (carbon 1) and compare it with the CH2OH group at the top left. That comparison is the key to this question.
Remember cellulose is made only from beta-glucose, where the OH on carbon 1 is on the same side of the ring as the CH2OH group. Alpha-glucose has them on opposite sides.
walkthrough:
**Recall the monomer**

Cellulose is a polysaccharide made by joining many glucose monomers with 1,4-glycosidic bonds. The special point is that it uses beta-glucose, not alpha-glucose.

**Spot beta-glucose**

In this ring drawing, carbon 1 is on the right and carbon 5 with CH2OH is at the top left. In beta-glucose, the OH on carbon 1 points up, on the same side as the CH2OH which also points up. In alpha-glucose, the OH on carbon 1 points down, opposite to CH2OH.

**Match to the diagrams**

Only diagram A has CH2OH up and the carbon 1 OH up together, plus all other OH positions correct for glucose. That is beta-glucose, so it is the monomer for cellulose.

options.A: Shows beta-glucose with OH on carbon 1 on the same side as CH2OH. This is the monomer joined to make cellulose.
options.B: OH position on the left side (carbon 4) is inverted compared to glucose, so this is not glucose, it is a different hexose like galactose.
options.C: Shows alpha-glucose with OH on carbon 1 opposite to CH2OH. This is the monomer for starch and glycogen, not cellulose.
options.D: OH position on carbon 2 is inverted compared to glucose, so this is not glucose, it is a different hexose.
